context: A radio talk about the Ashbourne Summer Festival

cues.t: Part 2. You will hear the organiser of a town's summer festival talking on local radio about this year's event. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.
Hello, and welcome to this week's Community Hour. I'm Moana Reid, and as chair of the organising committee I'm here to tell you about this year's Ashbourne Summer Festival.

The first thing to say is that the festival is growing. For the last five years it has run over two days, the Saturday and the Sunday. We did think about adding the Thursday as well, which would have made four days, but the stallholders weren't keen. So what we're doing instead is opening on the Friday, which gives us three days in all.

You'll also notice that we've moved from June to July. People have assumed that's for the weather, but in fact June is usually drier here. And it has nothing to do with the school holidays, which don't begin until the end of the month. It's simply that the county show has moved to our usual weekend, and we didn't want to be competing with it for visitors.

Tickets, then. A day ticket costs ten pounds, and that's the price whether you buy it online beforehand or at the gate on the day. I'm afraid we can't give refunds. But there is one good reason to book ahead: an advance ticket lets you use the car park without paying the usual three pounds.

So what's on? The children's circus workshop is back for the third year running, and it's as popular as ever. We had hoped to offer an open-air cinema, but the licence didn't come through in time, so that will have to wait until next year. What is completely new is a tasting tent, where you can try cheese, bread and honey from more than twenty local producers.

Finally, an appeal. We have plenty of people to sell programmes, thank you, and the traffic is being managed by a professional company this year. Where we're still short is on the Monday morning, when the whole field has to be cleared of litter. If you can spare a couple of hours then, please get in touch.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

Let me finish by describing the site, because it's been reorganised. There's a plan on our website, and you might like to have it in front of you. The main entrance is on the north side of the field this year, at the top of the plan, so you'll be facing south as you walk in.
The information point is the first thing you come to. As you walk through the main entrance, it's immediately on your left. That's where you can pick up a programme and ask about lost children.
The main stage is right in the middle of the field, as always. The first-aid post is beside the stage, on its eastern side, so that help is close by wherever you are.
The craft stalls have been moved away from the stage this year. You'll find them along the western edge of the field, about halfway down, which also happens to be the side nearest the car park.

All the food is now together in one big tent. It used to be next to the entrance, but the queues kept blocking the gate. So this year, walk right past the stage and keep going to the far end of the field. The food tent is in the south-east corner, beside the stream.
And lastly, the children's area. We wanted it well away from the noise of the stage, so we've put it in the south-west corner, in the shade of the big oak tree.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

items.stem: How long will the festival last this year?
The festival has been moved to July in order to

options.C: fit in with the school holidays.

items.stem: What is the advantage of buying a ticket in advance?

options.A: It costs less than at the gate.

items.stem: Which attraction is new this year?

groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 16–20.
